Here are my verse-by-verse notes for Mark 5:23–43, drawn from the approved sites. I note where sources were unavailable due to search limits.

---

## Mark 5:23–43 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 23 — Jairus’s urgent plea

Jairus, a synagogue ruler, falls at Jesus’ feet and begs Him urgently. Mark alone uses the affectionate diminutive **“my little daughter”** (θυγάτριόν, *thugatrion*), a touch of tenderness characteristic of Mark’s style. The phrase “lieth at the point of death” literally means “is at the last point” (*in extremis*). Jairus exhibits real faith in Jesus’ power, yet seems to think Jesus’ physical presence and the laying on of hands are necessary for healing — unlike the centurion of Luke 7, who believed Jesus could heal from a distance. Matthew’s parallel account has him saying she is “even now dead,” a summary compression of the event.

— Vincent’s Word Studies, Cambridge Bible, JFB, Gill, Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-23.htm
— Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 24 — Jesus goes with him; the crowd presses

Jesus responds immediately and goes with Jairus. The Greek verbs contrast: Jesus “went away” (aorist, a single decisive action), while the crowd “kept following” and “kept thronging” (imperfects, continuous action). The pressure of the crowd sets the stage for the woman’s desperate act.

— Vincent’s Word Studies: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-23.htm
— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html

---

### v. 25 — The woman with a hemorrhage

A woman had suffered from bleeding for twelve years — exactly the lifetime of Jairus’s daughter. This condition rendered her **ceremonially and socially unclean** under Leviticus 15:25–27, meaning she should not have been in a pressing crowd, let alone touching anyone. Eusebius records a tradition that she was a Gentile from Caesarea Philippi. The twelve-year parallel binds the two stories together: one woman suffered for the whole lifespan of the girl who now lies dead.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/5.htm
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 26 — The failure of human help

Mark piles up detail in a way the other evangelists do not, using a chain of participles to stress her desperation. She “had borne much agony,” spent everything, and only grew worse. Lightfoot’s *Horae Hebraicae* lists the remedies prescribed for such conditions — amply explaining why she grew worse rather than better. Spurgeon vividly expands: ancient physicians used cupping, leeching, cutting, cauterising, blistering, and “all manner of unimaginable tortures.” Her money was gone, her health was ruined, and all hope from human sources was exhausted.

— Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/5.htm
— Spurgeon, “The Touch,” Sermon 1382: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons23/sermons23.lii.html
— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html

---

### vv. 27–28 — The touch of faith

Hearing about Jesus, she comes behind Him in the crowd and touches His cloak. She “kept saying” to herself, “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” Her faith, while real, was arguably mixed with a quasi-superstitious notion — that Jesus’ power resided even in His clothing. Yet Spurgeon calls it “splendid faith”: “the point does not lie in the touch; it lies in what was touched.” She believed the faintest contact with Christ would suffice.

— Spurgeon: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons23/sermons23.lii.html
— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 29 — Immediate healing

“Immediately” (εὐθύς, *euthys*) her bleeding stopped, and she felt in her body that she was healed. Enduring Word notes the reversal: by Levitical logic, when an unclean person touched a clean person, the clean became unclean. But here, when the unclean woman touched Jesus, **she became clean** — He was not defiled. This pictures how Jesus takes our sin upon Himself and imparts His righteousness to us.

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/
— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html

---

### v. 30 — Jesus perceives power going out

“At once” (εὐθύς again) Jesus was aware that power had gone out from Him. Constable, citing Hiebert, stresses that Jesus’ healing power “did not work automatically, like a battery discharging its power when accidentally short-circuited.” Rather, “Jesus perceived in Himself, without any external suggestion, the significance of the woman’s touch, and, actively willing to honor her faith, He was immediately conscious of His healing power going toward her.” This suggests His healing ministry cost Him real spiritual energy, which may explain why He sometimes withdrew alone to pray.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 31 — The disciples’ incredulity

“You can see the crowd pressing in on You, and yet You ask, ‘Who touched Me?’” Mark alone records the bluntness of this reply. Luke identifies Peter as the spokesman (Luke 8:45). Constable suggests the disciples were impatient to get Jesus to Jairus’s house before it was too late. The question seemed absurd when the whole crowd was jostling Him.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 32 — Jesus looks around

He kept looking around to see who had done this. Jesus was not seeking information (He knew), but was drawing the woman out for her own good and for the benefit of onlookers — especially Jairus.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/7-jesus-heals-jairus-daughter-matthew-918-26-mark-521-43

---

### v. 33 — The woman’s confession

The woman “fell down before Him trembling in fear, and she told Him the whole truth.” Enduring Word explains that Jesus made her publicly confess not to shame her, but (1) to assure her she was not stealing a blessing, (2) to demonstrate to Jairus that faith — not magical touch — heals, and (3) to make clear that her faith, not the tassel, had healed her. The Pulpit Commentary adds that she may have feared Jesus would punish her with a return of her malady for having secretly drawn the blessing.

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/
— Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/5.htm

---

### v. 34 — “Daughter, your faith has healed you”

This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus addresses someone as **“Daughter.”** Her faith, not her touch, was the means. Constable notes the Greek verb *sōzō* (σῴζω) can mean both physical healing and spiritual salvation — a perfect active indicative implying she was healed and remained healed. Utley stresses: “There was nothing magical here, nor was it the power of positive thinking, but the power of Jesus.”

“Go in peace” (εἰς εἰρήνην) literally means “Go **into** peace” — not merely the absence of trouble but wholeness and well-being. “Be free of your affliction” uses a term derived from “to whip,” underscoring the torment from which she was delivered.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Utley (StudyLight): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/mark-5.html
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/5.htm
— John Piper, Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/my-little-daughter

---

### v. 35 — The devastating news

While Jesus was still speaking, messengers from Jairus’s house arrive: “Your daughter is dead; why bother the Teacher anymore?” Enduring Word imagines Jairus’s heart sinking: “I knew this was taking too long… Now the situation is beyond hope.” The interruption by the woman seemed to have cost Jairus everything.

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 36 — “Do not be afraid; just believe”

Jesus “overheard” (some manuscripts say “ignored” the messengers’ words). The Greek is literally **“Stop fearing; continue believing”** — a present imperative to cease one action and persist in another. Enduring Word notes: “Fear and faith cannot exist together in our hearts.” Spurgeon suggests that the healing of the woman was providentially timed to strengthen Jairus’s faith for this very moment: if Jesus could heal a woman with a twelve-year incurable haemorrhage, He could surely raise a twelve-year-old girl.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/
— Spurgeon: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons23/sermons23.lii.html

---

### v. 37 — The inner circle

Jesus permits only **Peter, James, and John** to accompany Him. Constable notes two reasons: (1) to limit popular reaction — if crowds thronged Him for healing, how much more if they knew He could raise the dead; (2) the principle of two or three witnesses (Deut 17:6; cf. Mark 9:2; 14:33). These three form what is often called Jesus’ “inner circle.”

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 38 — The commotion at the house

At Jairus’s house, Jesus finds “commotion and people weeping and wailing loudly.” Constable explains that, as was customary, **paid mourners** were already at work — weeping, wailing, singing, playing flutes, clapping hands (cf. Jer 9:17; Amos 5:16). The Mishnah required even the poorest husband to hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html

---

### v. 39 — “Not dead, but asleep”

Jesus declares: “The child is not dead, but asleep.” Constable clarifies Jesus used “sleep” **figuratively** for death, as He did for Lazarus (John 11:11–14). He meant her death would be no more permanent than sleep. Enduring Word connects this to Romans 4:17: God “calls those things which do not exist as though they did.” The mourners, however, took His words literally.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 40 — They laughed at Him; He clears the room

The mourners “laughed at Him” (κατεγέλων, *kategelōn* — they ridiculed or jeered). Their reaction, Constable notes, **proves the girl was truly dead**; they were not mistaken about her condition. Jesus “put them all outside” — He excluded unbelief from the room where He would display divine power. He took only the parents and His three disciples inside.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 41 — “Talitha koum!”

Mark preserves the very **Aramaic syllables** Jesus spoke: “Talitha koum!” — translated “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” Ellicott notes this is similar to Mark 7:34 (“Ephphatha”), where the Evangelist gives the actual Aramaic words that fell from Jesus’ lips and “had been proved to be words of power.” It would be too wide an inference to assume Jesus normally spoke Aramaic rather than Greek, but the stress laid on these Aramaic words shows they attracted special notice.

Jesus takes the dead girl by the hand. Constable notes that touching a dead person caused ceremonial defilement, but Jesus’ power overcomes it. Elijah (1 Kings 17) and Elisha (2 Kings 4) also raised children, but with far more effort; Jesus does it with a word. Piper (Desiring God) highlights the tenderness: Jesus picks up Jairus’s own affectionate language — “little girl” — showing “compassion and holy condescension.”

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/5.htm
— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Piper, Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/my-little-daughter
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

---

### v. 42 — Immediate restoration; utter amazement

“Immediately” (εὐθύς, used twice in this verse) the girl got up and walked. Mark adds that she was twelve years old. Constable draws the parallel: the woman had suffered twelve years and began living when she should have died; the girl died at twelve, just when she should have begun living as a young woman. Jesus delivers from both “deaths.”

The witnesses “were utterly astounded.” The Greek *existēmi* (ἐξίστημι) with the cognate noun literally means they were **“out of their minds with great amazement.”** Ellicott notes that Mark gives the age at the end of the narrative, Luke at the beginning, and Matthew not at all — evidence of a measure of independence among the Gospel writers.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/5.htm

---

### v. 43 — Strict orders of silence; “give her something to eat”

Jesus gives two commands. First, **strict orders that no one should know** — Constable explains this was to avoid unnecessary publicity so He could continue His ministry with maximum freedom of movement (cf. Mark 1:43–45). Gill adds that Jesus wished to avoid the envy of scribes and Pharisees, prevent crowds from trying to make Him king prematurely, and to show His dislike of ostentation.

Second, **“give her something to eat.”** This demonstrates she was truly alive and in normal physical health, not a ghost or spirit. Constable: “It also clarified that He had restored her to physical life that needed sustaining. He had not resurrected her to a new form of life with an immortal body (cf. 1 Cor 15:35–57).” Gill notes she was like one who had been asleep and was hungry upon waking — children of that age are typically hungry on rising. Ellicott observes that this detail (shared by Mark and Luke but absent from Matthew) suggests the fuller report came from an eyewitness present in the chamber. The Pulpit Commentary notes a gradation in Jesus’ resurrection miracles: Jairus’s daughter (just dead), the widow’s son at Nain (on the bier), and Lazarus (four days in the tomb) — each more dramatic, culminating in Jesus’ own resurrection.

— Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-5.html
— Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-5.html
— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/5.htm
— Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/5.htm

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

### Reformed / Evangelical (Don Carson, The Gospel Coalition)
Carson emphasises the **literary structure** of Mark 5:21–43 as a deliberate “sandwich” (intercalation): the woman’s story is inserted into Jairus’s story. Both involve females restored by Jesus’ touch; both feature twelve-year periods; both women are addressed tenderly as “daughter.” This is not accidental but a theologically driven arrangement by Mark under the Spirit’s guidance. The delay caused by the woman actually served to deepen the miracle for Jairus — Jesus is Lord over both chronic illness and death.
— https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/who-touched-me-mark-5-21-34/

### Reformed Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God)
Piper draws out the theme of **God’s fatherly heart**. Jairus’s cry “my little daughter” and Jesus’ “Little girl, I say to you, arise” reveal a tender, protective, fatherly affection. Jesus calls the older woman “Daughter” too — the only time in the Gospels He uses that address. The two stories side by side (vv. 34–35) show that both twelve-year-old girls and grown, suffering women need and receive the Father’s love through Jesus. This is not just about power but about the character of God.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/my-little-daughter

### Baptist (C.H. Spurgeon)
Spurgeon treats the woman’s faith as the central lesson — her “resolute determination,” “marvellous hopefulness,” and willingness to press through every difficulty. His sermon “The Touch” (No. 1382) stresses that the woman’s faith was not in the quality of her touch but in the **Object touched** — Christ Himself. He also highlights God’s providence: the woman’s healing was timed to prepare Jairus for the greater test of his daughter’s death. “A woman who led a living death is healed that Jairus may believe that his dead daughter may be raised to life!”
— https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons23/sermons23.lii.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word)
Guzik emphasises that Jesus’ power is **personal and relational**, not mechanical. He notes the woman’s faith was “mixed with superstition and incomplete understanding,” yet Jesus honoured it because “the object of faith — Jesus Himself — matters far more than the quality of faith.” He also stresses that Jesus felt power go out from Him — His healing ministry involved real spiritual energy and personal cost. The public confession was for the woman’s assurance, not her shame.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/

### Dispensational / Brethren (Hamilton Smith)
Smith reads the passage **dispensationally**: the demoniac sent into the swine pictures Israel scattered among the nations after rejecting Messiah; the dying child pictures Israel morally dead when Christ came; the child’s raising foreshadows Israel’s future revival at Christ’s return; and in the meantime, the woman represents **individual Gentiles** who obtain blessing by personal faith in Christ during the present age.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hsw/mark-5.html
